ME. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)  PRESS RELEASE RESPECTING NARCOTIC DRUG ADDICTION
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. Last night or some time yesterday while this house was sitting there was issued from the office of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) a press release entitled "A Statement of Hon. E. Davie Fulton, Q.C., M.P., Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada concerning narcotic drug addiction". This release starts out by saying:
The government of Canada has approved a comprehensive plan to deal with the problem of narcotic drug addiction in Canada, it was announced today by the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, Minister of Justice and the Hon. J. W. Monteith, Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The question of privilege to which I now address myself is one affecting all members of this house; a privilege which has been violated by the Minister of Justice in particular and, because of association by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
It is the practice and tradition of this house that while the house is sitting all announcements shall be made in the house and not outside it. I would suggest that because of his constant interventions on questions of procedure there is perhaps no one in this chamber who is more aware of this practice than the Minister of Justice.
On March 3 I addressed a question on this matter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, directing his attention to a statement made in British Columbia by the Minister of Justice that the government proposed to take concrete steps to make an effective attack on the narcotic drug traffic in this country. The Minister of National Health and Welfare replied simply: "No comment".
I addressed a question on this matter to the Minister of Justice himself on March 9, the reply to which certainly did not reveal the government's intentions. Then on March 10 again I directed a question on this matter to the Minister of Justice, who replied to my question in part by saying that he expected shortly to be in a position to lay certain tentative conclusions before his colleagues in 79951-0-249J
the cabinet and that "thereafter it might well be we would have proposals to make to the provinces." I then asked whether that would be this year, and the minister replied:
That I am not able to say, Mr. Speaker. The matter is a difficult and complicated one and it depends upon the rate of progress that we are able to make.
I submit that this important announcement on government policy should have been made in this house. To do otherwise would be a violation if made by any minister in these circumstances, but it is a particular violation when made by an hon. gentleman who holds himself out as a paragon of parliamentary virtue in this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can well understand the concern of the hon. gentleman in view of the past record of himself and his colleagues when they were on this side. Of course they are now prepared to strain at every gnat they can see flying in the air in an attempt to do something to redress the balance in the minds of the people of this country.
But if I may mix my metaphors I should like to point out to the hon. gentleman that he has laboured and brought forth a mouse, because there is really no question of privilege, nor has there been any departure from what I said I would do in answering the questions to which the hon. gentleman has referred. What was stated in the press release of yesterday, if the hon. gentleman would read it in a calm and dispassionate manner, is that the government has now approved in principle a certain new approach to the narcotic drug problem and has authorized the Minister of National Health and Welfare and myself to approach the provinces to enter into discussions with them with respect to these proposals.
That is exactly what I said would be done, in answer to the questions by the hon. member for Essex East which he himself has read. To that extent, therefore, the press release of yesterday indicated nothing new and took us no further than the point I had already indicated I hoped the government would be able to reach in the course of this year.
As the press release makes clear, until there are discussions and until the discussions with the provinces have been terminated and we are in a position to know the extent of

the provincial co-operation that may be forthcoming, we will not be in a position to determine our policy finally and state it to this house. At that time, when the discussions with the provinces have concluded so that we can put forward a definitive and comprehensive policy, this house will be informed, whether or not the hon. member for Essex East is in it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. A starred question in my name, No. 104, was passed as an order for return on April 6. The return was brought down on April 27. The questions were as follows:
1.	Is toxic nerve gas produced in Canada?
2. If so, (a) where; (b) since when; (c) for what purpose; (d) under what authority; (e) under whose jurisdiction; (f) to whom is it supplied; (g) on what scale?
The answers were:
1.	No.
2.	Not applicable.
On May 3, some six days later, the Toronto Star carried a press report which reads in part as follows, under the heading: "Canada Makes Nerve Gas":
Nerve gases and germ warfare agents are prepared from time to time by Canadian defence technicians in Canada in minute amounts, a defence research board spokesman said today. Neither type of warfare-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

I will provide it from the department of the Minister of National Defence, and this is my question of privilege. I feel I have to quote this in order to establish the question of privilege.
Neither type of warfare agent is produced or manufactured anywhere in Canada in quantities beyond laboratory amounts of a few ounces at a time the spokesman emphasized.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my office got in touch with the office of the Department of National Defence; a letter was sent to my office over the signature of the minister's executive assistant which said in part that the public relations officer of the Department of National Defence had made a press release available to the Toronto Star from which this report was taken. I have in my hand the enclosed copy of the press release, and on this pertinent point it reads as follows:
Nerve gases are not produced or manufactured in Canada but are prepared in very small research quantities-that is. in quantities involving a matter of ounces only. They are necessary in order to conduct research aimed at evaluating potential chemical warfare hazards and in improving defensive measures against them.
Question oj Privilege
My question of privilege is that the house was not given a full answer to this question that asked whether nerve gases were produced in Canada and on what scale. I feel that if the Department of National Defence, or the ministry, had wished to give parliament an adequate answer they could have given to this house-they should have given to this house-all the information that has been given to the press in this press release. My question of privilege, therefore, is that the House of Commons, that parliament itself, is entitled to full and frank answers and that members of parliament should not have to get replies to their questions supplemented by releases which subsequently appear in the press.

speechtext:
I have a question of privilege to deal with myself; this seems to be the day. Yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) brought before the house, quite properly I thought, the case of an apparent misuse of the stationery of the house, raised it as a question of privilege and presented a motion.
I have examined all precedents I could find in order to determine whether or not this amounted to a breach of the privileges of the house, without finding any precedent for it. It appears to me that it is not in that category and does not raise a prima facie question of privilege. I should just like to read from May one paragraph which outlines generally the privileges which have been established by precedent as those of the house. It will be found at page 109 of May's sixteenth edition. In it Campion states as follows:
It would be vain to attempt an enumeration of every act which might be construed into a contempt, the power to punish for contempt being in its nature discretionary. Certain principles may, however, be collected from the journals which will serve as general declarations of the law of parliament. It may be stated generally that any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any member or officer of such house in the discharge of his duty, or which has a tendency, directly or indirectly, to produce such results may be treated as a contempt even though there is no precedent of the offence.
This appears to be rather an administrative problem under the jurisdiction of the house through its Speaker and its officers and undoubtedly can be dealt with in that category rather than by straining the law of parliament to cover this particular incident.

speechtext: I should like to ask either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of state for External Affairs whether a statement could or should be made on recent events in Paris which have caused so much discouragement and anxiety.

speechtext:
The situation in Paris in regard to the summit meeting is still delicate and uncertain. Premier Khrushchev failed to attend a meeting with the western three this afternoon which had been designed to get the summit meeting started. The prospects are therefore not bright; but so long as the four heads of government are still in Paris there would be no value in my attempting to speculate on the possible turn of events. I have made known to our NATO colleagues our desire that this situation should be discussed in the council at the earliest opportunity, and we shall be able tomorrow to examine the situation with our NATO allies in the council, possibly together with one or more of the three western foreign ministers.
Whatever the outcome of today's meeting the Canadian government remains determined to do everything possible to make progress in the field of disarmament where we are particularly engaged, as hon. members know, and where the United Nations has a special responsibility.

the second reading of Bill No. C-61, to amend an act to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to learn during the resolution stage that all hon. members who spoke considered this to be good legislation. There were suggestions that more assistance should be provided from the railway grade crossing fund, particularly to the municipalities. I think the facts prove that the increase in the measure of assistance to municipalities from the fund in the past two years has been very important indeed.
The crossing problem is the concern of the federal authorities, the provincial and municipal highway authorities, and the railways. The provinces and municipalities require highways and railways and benefit from both, notwithstanding that crossing dangers accompany the benefits. Crossings are not the responsibility solely of the federal authorities. Nevertheless, it is my desire that federal assistance be provided in as generous a measure as is reasonable in the circumstances as they may be from time to time. Consequently I shall keep in mind the suggestions that have been made when considering what further measures may be appropriate in dealing with the crossing problem. It is a problem that will have my continuing and sympathetic interest at all times, and I welcome all suggestions made to deal with it.
There was expressed a very understandable desire to have railway cars painted or made reflective so they will be more easily seen at crossings in the night time, and there were requests for information as to what is being done to place reflective markings on the sides of railway cars, for which parliament has made money available from the railway grade crossing fund.
The board of transport commissioners issued a judgment and order on May 1, 1959

Railway Act
requiring the Canadian railways to place reflective markings on all new box cars received by them between that date and the end of 1960, and on an equivalent number of old box cars. Last year the Canadian Pacific Railway marked approximately 3,000 box cars with reflective "scotchlite" discs four inches in diameter. The larger cars have nine discs on each side, smaller cars have seven. The Canadian National Railways did not mark as many as the Canadian Pacific Railway, because they bought fewer new box cars than did the C.P.R. Canadian National Railways are using two different types of reflective discs. The board has been advised that the C.N.R. marked 696 cars in 1959.
The board expects that by the end of this year there will be approximately 10,000 cars marked. The board feels it is necessary to have experience with the markings under actual operating conditions before determining a longer range program.
As regards United States cars, I am informed that several bills were introduced in the United States congress with the object of requiring United States railway vehicles to be equipped with reflective or luminous material. One of them was suggested by the interstate commerce commission. Several such bills were considered in 1957 by a subcommittee of the House of Representatives, but to date none has become law. The interstate commerce commission has been informed of our legislation and the board of transport commissioners' order.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets) and the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) raised matters concerning the Canadian National particularly, and I have drawn their representations to the attention of the management.
One or two members suggested that crossing signs be made to stand out more prominently. The board has started a program of putting reflectors on railway crossing signs, and has designated some 2,141 priority crossings to be so marked in 1959 and will designate other crossings as progress is made. Grants of 80 per cent of the cost are made for this work from the grade crossing fund. Advance warning signs some distance from crossings have been erected by provincial authorities in a great many cases. Efforts are being made to have them uniform throughout Canada, and the joint committee on uniform traffic control devices has recommended that these advance warning signs be of uniform design of yellow and black reflector material.
There was also a suggestion that the investigation should be made to see whether the diesel whistle cannot be made more like

the steam whistle. The technical officers of the board, the railways, and the national research council engaged in studies of this problem, and tests were conducted with a view to having a diesel horn that will simulate the sound of the old steam whistle. Following this study the board issued an order which directed the railways to equip road service units with horns having certain tonal characteristics. It is, of course, difficult to simulate exactly the sound of the conventional steam whistle, and the present types of horns now in use are the closest to that aim it has been possible to produce up to the present time.
Last night the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) asked certain questions, and I have requested that answers be prepared by the board of transport commissioners. I will give the answers to the two hon. members as soon as they are received.
As I have said before, I am very much interested in the crossing situation and welcome all suggestions that are made for remedial measures. In conclusion I wish to express my thanks for the support which has been indicated for this measure.

My remarks in connection with this matter will be brief, because the house already knows the position which we on this side take. We support this measure as forward-looking legislation.
I believe when this act was amended some two years ago I had the opportunity of speaking at length on the whole question of grade crossing accidents in this country and the measures taken by previous governments, and this government as well, to put an end, so far as possible, to such accidents. To the extent that we in this house can assist, I am sure all members of parliament will wish to co-operate in the fullest measure.

the board travelled from one end of the country to the other, and finally made many excellent recommendations. Many of those recommendations were put into effect by the former administration. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 4 deals with the game ordinances in the Yukon. This brings up a particular problem which I think I should bring to the attention of the committee so there will be no misunderstanding in the passing of this clause.
In the Northwest Territories a resolution was passed last year asking the federal government to make clear the legality behind their right to pass ordinances on game matters. This we have done in the bill which we allowed to stand just a few minutes ago. The comments I was going to make on the Northwest Territories legislation I will now have to make on the Yukon legislation.
In the Northwest territorial council resolution the difficulty of the Indians and Eskimos in the territory was considered. I should like to explain the background of this difficulty, which is a matter of great importance to hon. members of this committee, because under treaty and under statute we are required to protect the livelihood of the native people who lived in Canada before the white man came. In most parts of Canada including the Northwest Territories there are treaties that protect the rights of the Indians, but there are no treaties to protect the rights of Indians in the Yukon. Therefore in considering this problem we had to keep in mind what protection could be given to the Indians in the Yukon.
This matter only arose because last year a judicial decision was handed down in the Northwest Territories which pointed out that in the opinion of the presiding judge the territorial council had no power to make game

ordinances in so far as they affected Eskimos. This put the game legislation in question. We had turned over the management of the game to the Northwest Territories in 1948. The territorial government had passed ordinances dealing with game, and now a judicial decision had put this jurisdiction in doubt.
As a result they met and passed a resolution calling on the federal government to amend the Northwest Territories legislation in such a way as to make clear without any doubt that they had power to deal with game matters. Then to make certain that they recognized that the interests of the Indian and Eskimo were protected, the last section of their resolution was framed in these words, which I wish to put on the record and to which I ask all hon. members to give their undivided attention because they have the traditional duty of protecting the Indian in Canada:
And further that the council undertakes that in all cases and at all times the basic rights of Eskimos and Indians to hunt and trap on unoccupied crown land shall be preserved and shall be abridged only to ensure the conservation of game animals as a continuing resource to such extent as is necessary for their livelihood.
This means that even though the federal government is amending the Northwest Territories legislation to give to the territorial government the right beyond all question to deal with matters concerning game, the territorial council gave this undertaking that the traditional rights of the Indians and Eskimos in the Northwest Territories would be preserved. If the amendment to the Yukon Act which is now before us is read carefully, the matter of the protection of Indians and Eskimos could be brought into question. Clause 2 reads:
Notwithstanding subsection (1), the commissioner in council may make ordinances for the government of the territory, in relation to the preservation of game in the territory, that are applicable to and in respect of Indians and Eskimos, and ordinances made by the commissioner in council in relation to the preservation of game in the territory, unless the contrary intention appears therein, are applicable to and in respect of Indians and Eskimos.
I am not a lawyer, but this simply means that you give to the Yukon council the right without question to make ordinances in relation to hunting by Indians and Eskimos, and the only exception to it is that clause where it says "unless the contrary intention appears therein".
Therefore in the Yukon, under this amendment to the act, the rights of the Indians and the Eskimos are exactly the same as those of the white man unless especially arranged for in their ordinances or in the regulations. The question that arises is this. Since there

is no treaty that usually guarantees to Indians the traditional right of hunting, are we doing anything, by giving to the territorial government this right to pass ordinances, that lessens the traditional right of the Indian to hunt for his livelihood? I raise this with the committee, because I would be prepared to entertain an amendment in the form of an additional clause which would make this right absolutely equal.
Here I might point out that there are other protections for the Indian and Eskimo. First, the legislative body, the territorial council, has the right to pass legislation, and the commissioner who is appointed by the federal government has the right to not sign that legislation. That is one control to make certain that the rights of the Indian and Eskimo are protected.
The second protection is the fact that all ordinances of the territorial governments must have the approval of the governor general in council, and this means the approval of the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. If these two protections are not sufficient, then the committee should seriously consider adding an amendment to clause 4 to make clear that the traditional right is not in any way abrogated.

should be placed on the food stores? How would that be made up if there were a limitation?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext:
Under my department there is the wildlife service of Canada which operates in co-operation with all the provinces, and of course it is responsible for the territories as well, even though the administration of game in the territories is now under the jurisdiction of the two territorial councils. The wildlife service of Canada periodically makes surveys of the amounts of various game in each part of the territories, and on the basis of that information the territorial government changes the regulations that look after the management of game in that area.
I might point out to the hon. member that in the north, owing to the climate and the lack of vegetation, in many parts game is not plentiful; it is a very scarce commodity. In the interests of the Indian and the Eskimo it certainly has to be regulated to give him any protection whatsoever. As the hon. member has probably heard, in the Northwest Territories, for example, the regulations for hunting and trapping severely limit the rights of the white man. The rights of the non-resident are for a very limited amount of game bird shooting; the rights of the resident white man are equally limited, and only under certain conditions is he allowed to take off big game.
In the Yukon game is more plentiful; therefore the regulations work equally for all, white man, Eskimo and Indian. But the power to regulate has to be in their hands, and it has been in the hands of the Yukon territorial council since about 1900. Therefore they have this right traditionally, like any other province, and they have had it for about 60 years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext:
The problem I am thinking of is that there are a great number of white men going into the north on development work. This may apply more to the Northwest Territories than to the Yukon, but it seems to me that if all the people in that area had equal rights it would probably give the white man an advantage, because he would be hunting for a purpose different from that of the Indian and Eskimo. If the white man were given equal right to kill game there we would be taking away from the Indian and Eskimo his means of livelihood. Certainly we want to conserve the game. It may be necessary to limit the numbers taken, but if this is done we have a responsibility to ascertain what the loss will be to the native population; we should be willing to

Yukon Act
make up to the native population something in kind, and obviously it would have to be something very definite in its application.
I am not sure whether the minister has said that the ordinance will apply to all people within the area in the same way. That would mean, would it not, that the white man would probably get an advantage under the regulations and the native population would suffer a disadvantage? I should like to see the native population protected by ascertaining what they would receive in kind, if this ordinance was passed, to make up for their losses, and how we would administer it and see that they receive this extra amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: The territorial council have administered game in the Yukon since the turn of the century. They have been very conscious always of the necessity of protecting their game, and they have done a good job. All this amendment does fundamentally is to make sure that there is no question about their right to pass these ordinances. They have had these ordinances in effect in the Yukon since 1900. However, as the result of decisions last year a doubt was created about this right, so this provision was inserted to give them this right beyond the shadow of a doubt. This provision makes the ordinances passed in previous years legal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: The point to which I am referring-I have not seen the ordinances-is that the ordinances may say every male over the age of 21 has the right to hunt and kill, say, one caribou, one moose or whatever it happens to be. Some of the native population are dependent on shooting not only one of these animals but perhaps half a dozen. It seems to me that the Eskimo would be put in a position of hardship by being given equality with the white man. In the past I presume that the Eskimos have been able to kill as much as they needed for food, and then the department made up the balance. By putting the Eskimo under this regulation it would seem to me he would be subject to the same kind of game limitation as the white man, and this would interfere with his ability to live off the land. In many cases the natives have to kill far more than any conservationist would allow in that area.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP
speechtext:
I think I have the point which the hon. member is making. Considerable work has been done by wildlife surveys in outlining what they call the sustaining yield which is possible for this type of animal and that type of animal. The ordinances simply set out the trapping areas to protect the individual person in the area

who has a trapping licence. Nearly all the trapping and hunting is done by Indians. There is only a handful of Eskimos in the Yukon. These provisions have worked well for 60 years, and game is reasonably plentiful. The difficulty of the trapper and the hunter in the Yukon is not that he cannot get game, but the fact that fur prices have declined so drastically he cannot sell his furs.
I think the answer to the hon. member's question is that the territorial government have managed this game very successfully for 60 years, and they have looked after the interests of the Indians under these ordinances. The government has carefully watched the white hunter, who is usually a professional hunter bringing in sportsmen to hunt the big game animals of the Yukon. Whenever a person in the Yukon, whether he is white, Eskimo or Indian, wants to hunt for food, these ordinances do not limit what he can do unless he wilfully slaughters animals beyond the capacity of the area to carry. Generally speaking, if a man wants food there is no limit on what he can do. subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO JULY 31, 1963
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary certainly has been brief in moving the amending bill. I am very anxious to commend him for that, but I am not sure that he may not have overdone it a little on this occasion. However, I do believe that this is the first occasion on which he has had the honour of presenting a bill in his new capacity of parliamentary secretary and I certainly want to extend my good wishes to him on this occasion.

Export and Import Permits Act
This legislation became necessary by reason of the last war. It was first brought forward under the authority of the War Measures Act and the emergency powers legislation, and some 13 years ago, in 1947, was brought forward under an act of this house directly related to the subject matter of the Export and Import Permits Act. That legislation, in the light of changed world circumstances and experience in operating the act, was amended and the amending legislation took the form in 1954 of a wholly new act. The 1954 act is the act with which we are presently concerned and it was first enacted for a limited period of time. In 1957 a three-year extension was provided, and this bill now before us provides a further three-year extension.
I think all hon. members will agree that this type of legislation is not the type of legislation which is desirable in our parliamentary system and that, were it not necessary, it should not be brought forward. I think hon. members will also have to agree that world circumstances being what they are today there is not much alternative left but to grant an extension of this arbitrary power given to the government to control exports for certain purposes and to control imports for certain limited purposes set out in the act. However distasteful that grant of arbitrary power to the government may be- and I think it is distasteful to all hon. members in the house-it regrettably is necessary, and I think if any evidence of that were needed it is provided by the events of these last few days.
The legislation itself provides for export control of certain commodities to all areas in the world and of all the commodities to certain areas in the world. There are two types of control, commodity control and area control. The real problem, of course, is the preservation of the security of our country and the control of exports for that purpose. I hope the parliamentary secretary will say what he considers the prospects are for any change in the export controls as they are presently applied by the orders in council authorized under the act and what, if any, recent changes have been made.
I understand from the annual report covering the period up to December 31, 1959 that there were no substantial changes in that year. However, I would ask the hon. gentleman to say when he is replying in this debate whether or not there have been any changes in the export controls during the period since December 31, 1959 and, if so, the nature of those changes and the reasons for them.
In the act, the extension of which is being sought, provision is made under the terms of section 5 as follows:
[Mr. Mcllralth.l

The governor in council may establish a list of goods, to be called an import control list, including therein any article the import of which he deems it necessary to control for any of the following purposes, namely,
(a)	to ensure, in accordance with the needs of Canada, the best possible supply and distribution of an article that is scarce in world markets or is subject to governmental controls in the countries of origin or to allocation by intergovernmental arrangement;
(b)	to implement any action taken under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the Fisheries Prices Support Act, the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act or the Agricultural Products Board Act, to support the price of the article or that has the effect of supporting the price of the article; or
(c)	to implement an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment;
The section further provides:
Where any goods are included in the list for the purpose of ensuring supply or distribution of goods subject to allocation by intergovernmental arrangement or for the purpose of implementing an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment, a statement of the effect of a summary of the arrangement or commitment, if it has not previously been laid before parliament, shall be laid before parliament at the time the order of the governor in council including those goods in the list is laid before parliament pursuant to the Regulations Act.
It will be seen that the circumstances requiring the control of imports have changed materially since this legislation was first brought forward in 1947. At that time the major problem was the problem of the sorting of goods. There was the necessity of distributing those goods which were in short supply so as to provide an equitable sharing of the limited quantities entering the country. That problem has largely, if not entirely disappeared. I point out that this represents the granting of a power, and that the authority to establish import controls has not been restricted in the amending bill. Indeed, I am wondering if there is still any need for the power granted in section 5 (a) of the act and whether or not there are any goods on the import control list under the provisions of that subsection.
Subsection (b), of course, has to do with the control of the import of articles in order to make the government's price support legislation, in one form or another, workable. The need for that power has probably increased during the years. For my part I should like to have the opportunity to examine this question to find out just how extensive a use has been made of the powers granted under subsection (b) of section 5 and I hope the parliamentary secretary will give us all the information he has on that point when he replies.
Section (c) has to do with intergovernmental arrangements or commitments. Again, I wish the parliamentary secretary would

explain what intergovernmental arrangements or commitments are still in existence at this date.
That brings me to a suggestion. The bill which is now before us is a very short and simple bill. It simply changes the expiry date of the act from July 31, 1960 to July 31, 1963, and it will be seen that according to a reasonably strict interpretation of the rules it would be impossible, or very difficult, for us to get the statistical and factual information which would be desirable during consideration of this measure by the committee of the whole. I am wondering if the parliamentary secretary would consider referring this measure to the banking and commerce committee in order that we might obtain statistical information on the points I have mentioned as well as other related points. I believe the whole matter would only require one sitting of the committee-I venture that opinion-during which time the information I have in mind could be made available. I think it is important that this should be done, because this is one of those pieces of legislation which are altogether unsound theoretically but which are, unfortunately, necessary. It is, therefore, the type of legislation which should be subject to detailed examination with a view to determining precisely what use is being made of it, and what present need exists for the powers granted. It is clear there is a need for the export control authority, but it is not so clear that the legislation is needed in respect of the import control authority.
I therefore conclude my remarks with a request that the parliamentary secretary give all the information he can, and that he consider referring the bill to the banking and commerce committee for consideration.

I listened with a good deal of interest to the comments of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). I had expected the parliamentary secretary in introducing the bill at this stage to give us a report on the operations of the Export and Import Permits Act, especially as it has been applied in more recent days, in order that we might more adequately be able to decide whether we ought to support the amendment to extend the operation of the act. However, our group intends to support the extension.
I endorse the recommendation made by the hon. member for Ottawa West that this bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce in order that we may undertake, possibly for the first time in the history of the act, a review of the operations of this legislation. I cannot agree with the hon. member when he expresses regret
Export and Import Permits Act for the necessity of the existence of the legislation. I am not too afraid of the government in announcing the intentions of the act. I am more afraid of the influence on the Canadian economy and security of the activities of individuals who operate primarily with a profit motive in mind than I am of arbitrary decisions by the minister who is admittedly granted much authority in the operation of this act.
We in this group regard this type of legislation as most desirable. It could be very useful as a method of regulating international trade, a method far in advance of the present method by means of tariffs. We believe that under this act, especially if it were expanded, the government could do a lot to protect not only the security interests of the nation but the economic interests of Canadian enterprise and the interests of producers and workers.
Under the act export licenses may be issued on arms and ammunitions provided they will not be potentially used against Canadians in any possible area of conflict. I wish the parliamentary secretary would report on what permits were granted within the last year for the export of arms and munitions and whether any have been issued to Central America, other Latin American countries and the Union of South Africa. I believe that report would interest all Canadians. This provision is useful in ensuring that there will be an adequate supply in Canada of items that may be desired elsewhere but that might otherwise be exported out of Canada leaving Canadians without the necessary supply.
According to the minister's annual report the export permit section is used extensively. In 1958 there were 8,199 export permits issued and 5,767 in 1959. In 1958 there were 700 applications refused, cancelled or withdrawn. Would the minister give an explanation as to what commodities the government decided against permitting to be exported under license.
The hon. member for Ottawa West placed on the record reasons for which the minister may refuse to grant import licenses, mentioning commodities in scarce world supply, refusal in order to protect agriculture in Canada and the intent of the Agricultural Stabilization Act and refusal because of arrangements existing with other governments.
I notice that the act is used for a wide range of commodities such as butter, cheddar cheese, butter fat, dry skim milk powder, turkeys and, until recently, tin. An import permit was needed if tin came from certain specified areas of the world. I believe this to be an indication of relaxing tariff barriers which

Export and Import Permits Act should be welcome only where an absence of export or import permits is a handicap to the development of international trade. We would like to see the act used more extensively than at present for the protection of Canadian enterprise. We hope the government will decide it is a more useful up to date system of regulating exports and imports than is our present outmoded tariff arrangement.
If the Canadian economy must import certain commodities I see no reason why the consumer should pay a tariff of any kind on the imported commodities. By wise use of this act in expanded form we could eventually abolish the tariff structure which presently controls exports and imports. The hon. member for Ottawa West is afraid of arrogance on the part of the bureaucracy or unwise decisions on the part of the government. I would recommend that the act be amended to allow an appeal by any individual or concern that feels that some civil servant or the minister has misused his authority and is not living up to the intent of the act. If there were an appeal procedure I believe the objection raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West concerning the need for the existence of the act would lose its entire validity.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
In preparing for the discussion of this particular bill I have been comparing it with other particular bills and I find a marked difference in the material and evidence presented before the committee of the other place. I think the difference is sufficient to allow for a rather exhaustive examination of some of the points mentioned in that evidence and perhaps some inquiry on the part of the committee here as to the facts or some of the things which I intend to relate. But first, perhaps, before we get into that phase of it, I should properly establish some of the things which are mentioned in the petition itself. One is that the marriage took place on September 6, 1949 between the petitioner and the respondent and that it took place in the city of Montreal. The petition also indicates that there is a judgment of the superior court of the province of Quebec given on December 10, 1952 with respect to separation as to bed and board but that there was no provision for alimentary allowance to the wife and also that there are no children born of this particular marriage. The petition indicates that adultery is alleged to have taken place on December 31, 1953 and on January 1 and January 2, 1954, some six years or seven years ago.
In attempting to relate the evidence in the order in which it appears to these particular parts in the petition perhaps we could deal first with the question of the marriage. The petitioner was called and sworn and was asked a number of questions by the clerk of the committee as to her name, age, occupation, place of residence, and so on. Then following these preliminary matters these questions were asked:
Q. Are you married? And if so, to whom?
A. I am married to-
Here she gives the name of her husband or the respondent.
Q. When were you married?
A. On September 6, 1949.
Q. Where?
A. In Montreal.
Then she is asked by whom and to what church her husband belongs and then we find the following questions:
Q. I show you a document. Do you recognize it?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. What is it?
A. My marriage certificate.
Q. Are the names and dates correct?
A. Yes.
Then the marriage certificate is filed and marked as exhibit No. 1. She is then shown a photograph which was taken on their wedding day or which she indicates was taken on their wedding day. This photograph is identified and filed as exhibit No. 2.

The references to separation may be of some interest to the committee because in the evidence at the point where separation is referred to-that is separation as to bed and board-there is also testimony as to the attitude of the husband toward his wife during the period of time they lived together or cohabited as man and wife. Incidentally, I may say, this was only a period of about two months. Questions then are asked.
Unfortunately, while Mr. Lieff, Q.C. of the city of Ottawa appeared as counsel for the petitioner, I do not find in the direct examination of the petitioner any reference or any passage where Mr. Lieff undertakes any questioning. It is recorded in the evidence that the clerk of the committee asked all these questions about where the husband was born and his occupation, about separation and so on, which normally, I understand, fall to the lot of the counsel who appears for the petitioner. I would therefore assume that this item has inadvertently been left out of the evidence and that Mr. Lieff does enter the picture in the questioning here at some stage, probably right after the identification of the photograph, although this fact is not indicated in the minutes.
The questioning then proceeded, as found on page 10. As I say, I think it would have been by Mr. Lieff, counsel for the petitioner, although the record does not show it.
Q. Did you live with him as man and wife?
A. Yes.
Q. Are there any children born of the marriage?
A. No.
Q. Until when did you live with him?
A. The end of October, 1949.
This is the reference as to the fact that they lived together or cohabited as man and wife for a very short period of time, namely from September 6, 1949 to the end of October, 1959 or a period somewhat less than two months. Then the questioning continues:
Q. Did you go to the superior court of the province of Quebec to get a separation?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you get a separation?
A. Yes.
Q. What sort of life did you have with him prior to that?
A. It was an impossible life because he changed after we were married. He had been a gentle, kind person, but he suddenly became very argumentative and it turned into physical abuse and he hit me several times. I was a widow with children and they were frightened of him. He abused them.
Q. In your action in the superior court did you complain about this physical violence?
A. Yes.
Then there is some questioning about the judgment of the court, alimony and so on. Questions are also asked about collusion, condonation and whether the petitioner entered into any of these arrangements to allow

for this divorce to be granted or to allow for the evidence to be presented, or whether she condoned the adultery complained of. These again are questions which, according to the evidence, were asked by the clerk of the committee but which I rather expect Mr. Lieff would be asking. The following questions were asked:
Q. Is there any agreement or understanding between you and him to get this divorce?
A. No.
Q. Have you schemed about the adultery or connived at it or arranged to bring it about?
A. No.
Q. Do you know-
Here he gives the name of the corespondent and the answers is no. The questioning continues:
Q. Were you with your husband on December 31, 1953 and on January 1, and January 2, 1954?
A. No.
Q. Have you lived with your husband as man and wife since the separation?
A. No.
Q. Has he supported you since the separation?
A. No.
Q. Are you working?
She says that she is. Then there are questions about having sufficient for her needs and general questions of that nature. Then we find the following:
Q. Is there any possibility or hope of reconciliation between you?
A. No, that is impossible.
Q. Have you forgiven him for the adultery you complain about in paragraph 7 of the petition?
A. No.
Q. Would you take him back under any circumstances?
A. No.
Q. Did you do what you could to make a success of the marriage?
A. Yes.

Then the chairman of the subcommittee, Senator Cameron, asks:
Q. Does this mean you lived with him less than three months?
A. Yes.
There is one thought I might express here. As I understand the law as it applies, if a wife is deserted and the desertion continues for a period of more than two years then she may sue for divorce stating as her domicile the place where she lives rather than the place where her husband lives. In this particular instance the petition is signed at Islington, Ontario, dated October 6, 1959. She indicates that she is living in the province of Ontario and that they have been separated since the end of October 1949, and that there has been a so-called legal separation, a separation from bed and board, from the superior court of the province of Quebec which was granted on December 10, 1952.

It would appear that perhaps those responsible for developing any alterations to our divorce law, if any course is taken with respect to these particular divorce cases arising from Quebec, might well consider-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member is now clearly in the realm of hypothetical and most unlikely developments. He is not arguing the case in issue.

If I might speak to the point of order, I would agree at first hand that it is not relevant to the case; but I do not agree that I am talking of hypothetical and most unlikely developments. I am merely suggesting that this would be a course of action for those who draft our laws to take in order that a woman in these circumstances might sue for divorce under her own domicile, in this case Ontario, instead of coming here with a petition. That concludes my comments on the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member mentioned that his remarks were not relevant to the bill. Therefore I would ask him to come back to Bill No. SD-45.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. In fact, when the hon. member for Halifax rose I was within a few words of completing my comments in that regard.
Testimony is given with respect to the allegation of adultery. It is not given by those who are classified as investigators and who make a practice of earning their living in this way because of unfortunate arrangements or strained difficulties between two people. It is testimony given by a man and woman who are man and wife, and who give in evidence that they witnessed certain things which occurred some six or seven years ago, on New Year's Eve, December 31, 1953 and on January 1 and 2, 1954.
Before we launch into considering this particular evidence I would like to express this thought, and perhaps the members of the committee can think about this and we might be able to come back to it and have some expression of opinion about it. Before I get into the evidence I may say in a general way that nowhere in the evidence, at least that I can find, is there any indication as to how the petitioner, how the lawyer, Mr. Lieff, if he did, or how anybody else in 1959-the petition is signed on October 6, 1959-had the knowledge that adultery existed some six or seven years before. Nowhere in the evidence, and I think this is a failure in it, can we find any indication as to why it took six or seven years for this particular circumstance, which it is alleged took place on New

Private Bills-Divorce
Year's Eve of 1953 and on January 1 and 2 of 1954, to come to light.
I think this should have been inquired into before the bill reached this particular stage. I think it should have been properly gone into in the committee of the other place in order that this unknown quantity be cleared up. There certainly is the question of delay in presenting this petition. If the petitioner knew some six or seven years ago that this incident took place, there appears to be a six or seven-year delay before filing her petition for divorce. If she did not know, then I think one is entitled to clear that question up and inquire as to when and under what circumstances it came to light.
As I say, I mention that because it is a point which we can go into later in order to clear up the question in my mind as well as perhaps in the minds of other members of this committee.
In any event, a gentleman who is not classed as an investigator, who describes himself as a salesman, is called to give evidence. His wife also appears to have the sedentary occupation of housewife. This gentleman, Mr. McDonough, is called and sworn and questioned by Mr. Lieff. Starting at page 11 the following questions by Mr. Lieff are recorded:
Q. Did you receive a subpoena to attend this hearing?
A. I did.
Q. Did you receive expense money-conduct money?
A. I did.
Q. I show you a photograph, which is exhibit 2. Can you identify the person of whom that is a likeness?
A. Yes, that is-
Then he gives the name of the respondent.
Q. Do you remember New Year's Eve, December 31, 1953, and January 1 and January 2, 1954?
A. I do.
I would think he has an exceptionally good memory, Mr. Chairman, unless there were a sufficient amount of memory searching to come up with these particular facts and be so positive about them. I continue:
Q. Do you remember where you were on those days?
A. Yes, we were at Rustic motel, in the province of Quebec.
Q. When you say "We", whom do you mean?
A. My wife and I and a few other couples were there over the January week end.
Q. You and your wife and a few other couples spent the holiday week end there?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know where-
-giving the surname of the respondent-
-was during the same week end?
A. Yes, he was with us.
Q. Was he alone?
A. No.
Q. Do you know who accompanied him?
A. Yes.
Q. Who?
A. A girl by the name of-
Then he gives the name of the corespondent. I would point out that up to this time at no place in the evidence is there any identification of this particular girl, the corespondent. Nobody says they know her, and in subsequent questioning no one asks the question: how do you know this was the name of the girl? Nowhere is it stated in the evidence that Mr. McDonough knew the girl, or asked her her name in order to find out what it was. It is just given as a statement of fact. This is a strange situation. I am not suggesting that Mr. McDonough did not know what her name was. I am only suggesting it is strange that it does not appear in the evidence how he came to know what her name was. In every case I can recall of this nature the investigators ask the name of the woman involved. Invariably they ask: what is your name? They have to know the name in order to serve the person concerned with papers, and so they can give the assurance that everything is aboveboard and that no skulduggery has taken place. In this particular instance, however, the name is given as a bald statement of fact and no elucidation follows. This, to my mind, represents a failing in the method which was used to obtain evidence before the committee of the other place.
The questions by the clerk of the committee continued:
Q. How many nights did you sleep there?
A. Three.
Q. Do you know where-slept on those nights?
A. I sure do.
Q. Where?
A. Right next door to us.
Q. What was the situation in that room?
A. Well, he was with this-
Then he gives the name-the name of the corespondent-as a bald statement of fact without any indication how he knew what her name was. That, I think, represents a failure in presenting the evidence in the proper fashion so that it can be properly assessed by the committee of the whole house here. This, coupled with a memory of six or seven years ago as proof of adultery, makes the situation even more strange. The questioning continues as follows:
Q. Were you in the room-that room?
A. Yes, we were.
Q. At what hour?
A. We were there in the morning.
Q. Each morning? Which morning.
A. New Year's morning.
Q. What did you see there?
A. Freddie.
Q. Freddie who?
A. Freddie

and this girl Ginette.
Q. How were they disposed?
A. They were dressed in pyjamas.
Q. Both of them?
A. Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to intervene briefly in this debate because, as I pointed out before and must point out again, when cases are under discussion in this committee the parties involved will have one defender at least, and possibly other defenders, against remarks made against them. I will refer only to the hon. member's remarks about Mr. Lieff. If there has been any question about the way Mr. Lieff carried out his duties in this case I know that the hon. members of the committee of the other place would have been very quick to find such fault with him and to bring him rapidly to judicial heel.
In reading this case any fair-minded man would, I think, agree with me that it was properly handled by Mr. Lieff and that no aspersion can be cast upon this always eminent counsel.
I wish to join with the hon. member for Halifax in his expression of protest. The business of character assassination in some quarters by some men is taken altogether too lightly.
Why not name names?
Yes, I intend to. I simply do not remember the constituency which the hon. gentleman who interrupts represents. That is the only reason I have not referred to him.
Skeena.

Thank you. The member for Skeena too lightly attempts to assassinate characters which is a despicable course of action especially when the person about whom he is talking is not present in the house to defend himself. The hon. member has now cast an aspersion on one of the most reputable members of the bar who has practised his profession for some 35 years and has considerable experience in appearing before the

committee of the other place. There has never been the slightest question about the character of Mr. Lieff nor has there been any suggestion about his having been lax. This distinguished counsel has always performed his duties in an outstanding manner. He is an eminent counsel. I rise in protest against the light way in which attempts are being made to reflect upon the characters of honourable men who over the years have earned the reputation of being honourable. I do not object to the hon. member for Skeena dealing with the matter in hand but in order to support the position he has taken he should not find it necessary to indulge in specious character assassinations.

Both hon. members who have spoken have been guilty of an assassination of my character, the latter hon. gentleman in more drastic terms. I have never taken advantage of being in parliament to say anything about anyone. Anything I have said about Mr. Lieff I am prepared to say not only inside the house where he cannot defend himself but outside the house as well where we meet on equal terms. I say again I think Mr. Lieff was lax and I will go further and say if he was not then the hon. members of the committee of the other place were lax and I know I will be called to order for casting aspersions on them.

And so forth. It seemed to me, in reading that, instead of giving the more proper name of Frederick, the witness, Mr. McDonough, indicated that he knew this Freddie quite well, and that was the explanation. A few lines further down Mr. McDonough says:
My wife and I and a few other couples were there over the January week end.
I think an inference can be drawn from that. My hon. friend has drawn an inference, but there is another inference possible, namely that they attended a sort of joint venture. These were the thoughts that came to my mind and they undoubtedly came to the minds of the people who heard the case in the other place, and therefore they did not go into the matters that my hon. friend has brought out.

I am glad the hon. member has elucidated it in that way. These are the thoughts that went through my mind, and

the inference could also be drawn that the witness indicated that this chap was an acquaintance of his, and that is how he came to know this person's name. This is an inference that can be drawn from the evidence; but we can infer other things, if this were a joint venture and the couples went up there for the week end. One could very well draw an unkind inference, perhaps, which I would not want to do, as to the relationship between any two of the other couples, and so on. But I still pose this question to the hon. member for Halifax, which I hope he will be able to clear up. Does he not think it would be better to have direct evidence, instead of having to draw an inference, as to how this individual, the husband, who appears as a witness, came to know this particular person's name?

Mr. Chairman, one is always faced with a difficulty when one examines a printed record rather than seeing the temper of the witness. As far as the printed record is concerned, I think my hon. friend is right. If the witness gave a good appearance before the Senate and even were he to pick up the photograph and identify it, whether it was done in an offhand manner or in a studied manner, the atmosphere at a trial does have its effect in determining whether you have an honest witness before you or one whom you have to check pretty closely. I think that on reading the evidence here of both Mr. and Mrs. McDonough one has to come to the conclusion that obviously the people who heard the case were satisfied they had two honest and reliable witnesses before them.

If I may deal with the apparent honesty of the witnesses, I have no way of questioning it whatsoever; I merely inquired of the hon. member, and he has answered in the affirmative, whether, in reading the evidence, it would be better to have this cleared up, and the hon. member for Halifax has agreed. I appreciate very much that he has agreed with me that Mr. Lieff was a bit lax in his duties in questioning-
I did not say that.

No; I did, and this is precisely where these questions and answers lead us. This is exactly what I was getting at in the first place. I say it now, and I will say it outside the house, Mr. Lieff was a bit lax. I used that word before; I use it now, and this is precisely what I was getting at. If this stirs up the blood pressure of the hon. member for Cartier and Sir Galahad from Halifax, I still say that Mr. Lieff was lax in his responsibility in not drawing this out

in the discussion so that this information will be brought out in a direct way in future cases.
May I carry on with the evidence? Following the evidence of Mr. McDonough, a witness on behalf of the petitioner is recalled and asked some questions by Senator Cameron as follows:
Q. Is Mr. McDonough, the witness who has just testified, related to you?
A. No.
Q. Is he related to Mr.-?
A. No.
This is a new venture in evidence in these matters as far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, but I assume this may have been done to clear up any doubt in the minds of the members of the committee of the other place as to the weight they should give to the evidence of Mr. McDonough. Perhaps the hon. member for Halifax will clear this up for me if I relate the assumption and ask him whether it is correct or not. I would assume that if the witness, Mr. McDonough, was related to the petitioner or to the respondent it would affect matters. Would this, not because of the inference that might be drawn by a favourable witness, if such a relationship did exist between Mr. McDonough and either the petitioner or the respondent, affect in any way the evidence? Is it possible for a relative to appear as a witness?

I think the answer to that is not as great weight is attached. If there was any doubt as to Mr. McDonough's evidence there might have been more cross-examination of him or more cross-examination of his wife. This is quite normal judicial practice to help determine how much weight should be given to a particular witness. The witness in this case answered that he was not a relative and the court did not proceed with any further cross-examination of Mr. McDonough.

Following that, with respect to the evidence in support of the petitioner, Mrs. McDonough, the wife of the person who was the last witness, appeared. On page 12 she gives evidence with respect to the circumstances. Mr. Lieff asks these questions:
Q. Do you know Mr. John McDonough, the last witness?
A. He is my husband.
Q. Please look at this picture, exhibit 2. Can you identify the person there?
A. Yes.
Q. Who is it?
A. Freddie.
Then she gives the name of the respondent. The next question is:
Q. Would that be-
Then, Mr. Lieff gives the full and correct name of the respondent, and her answer is
Private Bills-Divorce
in the affirmative, giving the same name. Then, these questions are asked:
Q. Do you remember New Year's eve, December 31, 1953?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. And January 1st and 2nd, 1954?
A. Yes.
Q. How do you happen to remember these dates?
A. It was the New Year's week end. There were five couples up north on that week end.
Q. Where did you stay?
A. At the Rustic inn.
Q. Do you know where the others stayed?
A. They all stayed at the Rustic inn.
Q. Where was-
Then, he gives the name of the respondent.
A. He had the room next to ours.
Q. Were you in that room?
A. Yes.
Q. How many beds were in that room?
A. One.
Q. Do you know where he slept?
A. In the bed.
She is assuming he did, I am quite sure of that, in view of the circumstances and the evidence she gives later. It is rather a direct statement to say that he did sleep in the bed.
Q. In that room?
A. Yes.
Q. Did he sleep alone?
A. No, someone was with him.
Again we come to the same point we dealt with earlier, Mr. Chairman.
Q. Who was that?
Then she gives the name of the corespondent. I have the same remarks to make with respect to Mr. Lieff's laxity in questioning this witness as I did in connection with the preceding witness, a laxity incidentally, with which I believe the hon. member for Halifax, agrees.
No, I would not like that to go unchallenged on the record. I definitely disagree.

I have not been in attendance at one of these divorce proceedings in the other place, but I assume that all the witnesses are excluded from the hearing, and each new witness is brought in as he is needed. This is the normal procedure in a court of law. I think Mr. Lieff, in his initial questioning of Mr. McDonough, brought out how Mr. McDonough happened to know the corespondent's name. Mrs. McDonough, who had not heard the evidence given previously by her husband, should have clarified that point and explained how she knew this particular girl's name. Then, there is further questioning:
Q. Were you in that room more than once?
A. Yes, every morning.
It is a very slight point, but there is some difference between her evidence and that of her husband. When Mr. Lieff asked Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Private Bills-Divorce
McDonough if he had been in that room he said, yes, we were there New Year's morning. His wife says that they were there every morning. It is a very slight point. Undoubtedly, they could both be correct because one could be there every morning and the other could be there just one morning.
Q. During the mornings when you were there, what did you see?
A. I saw-
She gives the name of the respondent and corespondent, and says they were in pyjamas.
Q. What was the condition of the bed?
A. It had been slept in.
Q. Please look at the petitioner. Is she the woman who gave her name, as so-and-so?
A. No.
There is the question of remembering events of some six or seven years ago. One might infer that these five couples were all good friends and knew each other very well, and this was some sort of a surprise. Mr. McDonough said it was. Perhaps this is the reason they remember that particular day so well.
There is one thing which I mentioned earlier, and that is the question of the time lag between the date of the allegation when adultery took place, that is December 31, 1953 and January 1st and 2nd, 1954, and the time when the petition was filed, which was in the latter part of last year. I feel that this question of the time lag should have been cleared up before the committee of the other place, but perhaps it could be cleared up in some way before we finally pass this particular bill. We know, for instance, if there is any undue delay in a court procedure between the time when the adultery took place and the time when the suit for divorce is entered, the court looks somewhat askance at the request and wants to know why there has been this undue delay. In so far as the evidence is concerned, this fact is not only unclear but there is no evidence as to when the petitioner gained knowledge of the adultery which took place some six or seven years ago. There is no evidence as to whether she had knowledge of this shortly thereafter-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO JULY 31, 1963
speechtext:
We know the nature of the intergovernmental arrangements with regard to this list under section 3(a). But with regard to section 3(b), I was rather surprised to find that pork was under export control under legislation that was enacted by parliament at a time when there was an acute shortage of goods and it was necessary to establish export control for military reasons

in order to protect the security of the country. I want to find out to what extent, if any, section 3(b) has been used for commodities other than commodities of a strategic or military nature.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO JULY 31, 1963
speechtext:
Yes. But the original legislation provided for import controls for that reason. As far as I am aware there was no suggestion that export control would have to be used for that purpose. I am somewhat uncertain as to why we required export control on pork at a time when farmers were complaining of the lack of markets for pork and the government itself had huge surpluses of pork on the market. It is just that narrow point to which I make reference and I should be glad if we could have it clarified.
Mr. Pallet!: There is no suggestion, except in what the hon. member has said, that this limits the market in any sense of the word. Quite often intergovernmental arrangements can expand the market by moving into the market on conditions that are well known and by co-operating with them can sometimes enlarge the market to a large extent. We therefore cannot accept the inference contained in the hon. member's remarks to the effect that the market is contracted. I suggest that this arrangement enlarges it. It is certainly within the purview of this act, section 3(b) to which the hon. member has referred, to have such an arrangement as has been worked out.

speechtext:

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO JULY 31, 1963

Is the list separate as between sections 3(a) and 3(b)?
Mr. Pallet!: No, it is not.

This was obviously created under this legislation to control the export of strategic materials and to ensure that arms, ammunition, etc. having a strategic nature might not be available to any destination where its use might be detrimental to the security of Canada. That was the original purpose of the legislation. I seem to have
Export and Import Permits Act stumbled on the fact that this arbitrary authority given to governments may be used for the purpose of controlling a somewhat doubtful agricultural policy of the government relating to farm commodities. subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO JULY 31, 1963

Would the parliamentary
secretary tell us if any exporter of these agricultural products has applied for a permit to export them to a foreign market and has been refused that permit?

Cuts were constructed and docks built with the result that there are facilities at the present time in the town of Objibway for ships. Between that portion of the town of Objibway where these facilities exist and the boundaries of the city of Windsor lies an area which is readily adaptable for harbour development and we believe that this harbour development should be undertaken in an orderly manner and under 79951-0-252
Windsor Harbour Commissioners Act direction; and that for this reason the territorial limits of the present harbour commission should be extended further down stream to include this additional area.
The minister has indicated that when and if this bill receives second reading it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I wonder if I would be presumptuous in suggesting that instead of referring this bill to that committee it be considered in committee of the whole at this time with the consent of the minister and of the house. Although the implications of the amendment may be quite extensive in that it increases the area over which the harbour commission has jurisdiction no other amendment is being made to the provisions of the act. I see no need for referring this bill to the standing committee and think it could well be dealt with in committee of the whole house this evening and perhaps receive third reading.

Mr. Speaker, while the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) is our shining lighthouse and harbour master, I want to make a few points. I wish to support the comments of the previous speaker and urge the minister to give full answers to the questions raised particularly with respect to representation of persons included in this greater area.
I wish also to compliment the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) for his short talk on this bill which is of great importance to his constituency. I noticed that the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer) said when he got up that he was not as verbose as the hon. member for Essex East but both spoke for approximately 15 minutes and I could not see much difference.
I think the hon. member for Essex East made a good point when he was questioned about being out of order and said that you cannot extend the area of jurisdiction of any board without extending its powers. That is a valid argument and he made an excellent case.
This is another illustration under the stresses of changing conditions and circumstances of extending the area of public planning and control. Anyone who has read the debates of this house of many years ago with respect to harbour commissioners and developments of that kind will remember that the Tory element in the community resisted that kind of development. This is a demonstration in a local sphere of a segment of C.C.F. policy.

the second reading of Bill No. S-5, to incorporate the Oshawa harbour commissioners.
He said: An interdepartmental committee comprising engineers and economists from the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works investigated the development of Oshawa harbour that might result from the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. It was found that although there might not be an immediate requirement for harbour works outside of dredging, the harbour being located only 17 miles from Toronto would be likely to develop by the establishment of industries requiring marine transport.
The city of Oshawa made formal application recommending the incorporation of harbour commissioners and would provide harbour front property, owned by the city, for management and development by the commissioners.
My department operates the government wharf that is used in the handling of coal, fuel oil and gravel from which a gross annual income of $18,000 is derived. The wharf would be placed under the management of the commission and the revenue would accrue to it.
The purpose of the bill is to set up a harbour commission to operate the harbour. There will be three commissioners, two appointed by the governor in council and one by the city of Oshawa. The bill is similar 79951-0-252J
Oshawa Harbour Commissioners in every detail to the one passed in April, 1957, to incorporate the harbour commissioners for Windsor, Ontario.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
