speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second such bill that has been brought to the attention of the house tonight and I see that there are others on the order paper, I rise to support the bill of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and in so doing may I say there are one or two points that I should like to bring to his attention as well as to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) because, unless I mistake the position of the two ministers, the Minister of Transport is responsible for the harbour commission that will be established under this bill and the Minister of Public Works is responsible for harbour facilities that may be erected by this harbour commission.
I think the House of Commons should know what plans are in the minds of the ministers, but more particularly in the mind of the Minister of Public Works in so far as the development of these harbours is concerned, arising out of the St. Lawrence seaway. It has been said repeatedly by this administration, as well as by the former administration, that the St. Lawrence seaway was going to have the effect of opening up many harbours. This statement is certainly confirmed by port facilities that are being built on the United States side of the great lakes and of the St. Lawrence. Before this bill is passed we would have some intimation, some inkling, from the government as to what its policy is with reference to this.
This brings me to a matter which I raised in the house and in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines two years ago when I submitted to the Minister of Transport and to the members of that committee that an economic survey should be made by the officers of the Department of Transport with reference to the impact which the St. Lawrence seaway would have upon the various regions of Canada. I repeated that in the house on two or three occasions and very little attention was paid by the Minister of Transport.
I say to the minister that of course he listened very carefully to what was said but absolutely nothing was done with respect to the recommendation. I understand that my colleague, the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), has put on the record the recommendation which was made by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in its

Oshawa Harbour Commissioners report in 1958, and I should like to put it on the record at this time. It is to be found at page 150 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee of 1958:
The continued close co-operation between the department, the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission toward the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project was noted with satisfaction. The importance of the seaway and its beneficial effect on Canadian inland ports was recognized by your committee, and a recommendation that municipalities which expect to enjoy maximum benefits from the project should survey existing port facilities and endeavour to determine necessary additional requirements, received the general support of members. The committee recommends for the consideration of the department the establishment of an economic survey to consider the effects of the St. Lawrence seaway project upon all regions of Canada.
If that had been done either by the St. Lawrence seaway authority or by the economics branch of the Department of Transport a great deal of misgiving would have been spared the various regions of this country. I can think of the Atlantic region; I can think of the region which is on the south shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, in the Gaspe area; I can think of the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, in the province of Quebec, where there is a tremendous amount of industrial development going on; and I can think particularly of the whole upper St. Lawrence from the international section right up to the foot of lake Ontario which, of course, includes the city of Oshawa.
Before a bill of this nature is passed it is essential that the city of Oshawa should have some idea of what the economic effect of the seaway is going to be on that port as well as on the other ports of the great lakes. It is known in the United States; it is known by a number of surveys that have been made there, as I will indicate on another occasion, not this one, what the effect of the seaway is and, because it has been known, large sums of money have been spent, for instance, in Milwaukee, in Duluth, in Chicago, in Buffalo, tremendous sums of money for port facilities, awaiting the movement of foreign-going vessels up the great lakes. But what have we done?
I made a motion in the House of Commons the other day for the production of a report from the Minister of Public Works as to what had transpired between the international section and the foot of lake Ontario. The minister opposed the motion and would not produce the report so that the house could know, so that Canada could know, what the officers of this department were doing about the development, industrial or otherwise, arising out of this new seaway and what effect it would have upon the various areas.

I could point to two such surveys which were made in the United States. I have one in mind now which is directly opposite the shore which extends from the international section at St. Regis right up to the foot of lake Ontario. On the Canadian side we have absolutely nothing, but on the United States side every port extending from Rooseveltown right up to Oswego has been surveyed and publicized with all sorts of information and data to give to the public to encourage industry to go there, as well as to encourage the state in case they should be interested in developing port facilities in that area.
It is a good thing to set up this commission. I am sure it will be a good thing for the city of Oshawa. I am sure that Oshawa wants it. But to what extent do we, in this country, know what the effect of the seaway will be on the Canadian side of the line? I believe that before very long this government will have to come to the conclusion it will have to spend large sums of money in order to assist industry to establish itself in these areas.
